Title: Monday Minute: mid-summer cutbacks
Notes: Banked Monday Minute: deadheading and cutting back for a second flush, what to do this month. Confirm one is banked from S1/S2.
Caption:
A border in the second week of July can look like it has already given its best. Half the perennials are going over, the colour is thinning, and the instinct is to leave it and wait for autumn.

Cut it back now instead. Hardy geraniums, catmint, Alchemilla and the early salvias will push a fresh mound of foliage and a second flush of flower if you take them hard back to the base once the first flush is spent. Keep deadheading repeat-flowering roses and dahlias so the plant spends its energy on new bud rather than setting seed.

Where it goes wrong is timidity and haste in equal measure. Cut too lightly and you leave a tired, half-spent border with no reason to break again. Cut everything to the ground and you lose the seedheads and structure you wanted to carry the autumn. The skill is knowing which plants repeat and which are earning their keep by going over.

Done at the right moment, a midsummer cutback buys a garden a whole second season.

Title: Monday Minute: spec-list landmines
Notes: Michael, 60 seconds banked at S2. The four checks every designer should run before signing off a semi-mature spec — the most common cause of a delivery that does not match the quote, named on screen.
Caption:
When a semi-mature delivery does not match the quote, the fault is almost never in the plant. It is in the four things the spec left unsaid.

Girth before height. UK nursery stock is measured by girth, the stem circumference at one metre, not by height alone. Two trees of the same height can be a caliper apart in presence and in price. Spec the girth and the height together.

Clear stem. If you want a clean standard, state the height of clear stem you need below the crown. Leave it off and a feathered, low-branched tree can still meet the height on paper.

How it is grown and supplied. Rootballed, containerised and air-potted trees of the same girth establish differently and cost differently. Name the one you are quoting against.

Form and stem count. On a multi-stem, state the minimum number of stems and the habit you want. Multi-stem with no number can arrive as two.

Get those four onto the spec and the tree that turns up is the tree you priced. Everything we quote is measured and described against exactly these points before a number goes near it.

Title: Monday Minute: holiday-week watering
Notes: Banked at S2: what dies in August and how to stop it before you go away.
Caption:
The plants that die in August are almost always the ones planted this year.

A tree or shrub in its first summer has not yet put roots out beyond the hole it went into. It is living on a rootball the size it arrived with, through the hottest, driest weeks of the year, and it cannot reach for water the way an established plant can. Leave it for a fortnight while you are away and it does not wilt and recover. It goes past the point of return.

Before you go, soak the rootball slowly and deeply, not the surface, so the water reaches the roots that matter. Mulch to hold that moisture in. Move containers out of full sun and group them together. On a new tree, a slow-release watering bag will drip-feed the rootball far better than a neighbour with a can.

The one thing to avoid is a light daily sprinkle. It wets the surface, draws the roots up to find it, and leaves them more exposed than before. In this heat, a plant is made or lost on how it is watered through its first season.

Title: Root pruning, explained
Notes: Shot at S4: why field stock gets root-pruned before lifting season. Hands in frame, Michael's voice from the bank over the top.
Caption:
Months before a tree is lifted, its roots are cut back by hand.

It sounds like the wrong thing to do to a plant you want to keep. It isn't. Cutting the long anchor roots now forces the tree to grow a dense mass of fine feeding roots close to the stem, the roots it will travel with. By autumn, when it comes out of the ground, it lifts with everything it needs to start again somewhere new.

Title: What a Creepers-grade scheme involves
Notes: Pinned quarterly anchor: one detail photo plus a plain breakdown of what goes into a scheme at this level. Filters tyre-kickers, ends on one quiet enquire line.
Caption:
A scheme at this level is not a delivery. It is years of work you never see on the day.

The specimens are grown on in open ground for a decade or more, then root-pruned a season ahead so they build a rootball dense enough to move. They are lifted in winter while dormant, craned in whole, planted, staked against wind-rock, and returned to through the first seasons until they stand on their own.

That is what the cost holds. The planting day is the smallest part of it.

None of it is negotiable, because none of it is optional.

Title: Monday Minute: order now for October
Notes: Banked at S6: why autumn planting wins, what to reserve this month.
Caption:
The best time to plant most trees and hedging is not spring. It is autumn.

By October the soil still holds the warmth of summer while the air has cooled and the plant is heading into dormancy above ground. Roots carry on working in that warm soil through autumn and into winter, so the tree spends the quiet months establishing rather than holding a canopy through heat. By the time next summer's dry spell arrives, it has a full season of root growth behind it and asks far less of you to keep alive.

The stock worth having is reserved long before it is lifted. The strongest semi-mature specimens and the cleanest hedging lines get spoken for through late summer, committed to schemes well ahead of the autumn rush. If you are planting in October, this is the month to walk the rows and tag what you want held.

Send your plant list to the office and we will reserve your specimens for the lifting season.
